extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and students of rhetoric interested in producing 'the sublime' style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing sublime, moving speech or elevated prose by using rhetorical figures, arrangement, and stylistic devices; includes warnings about audience, restraint, and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath must suit context
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere swearing of an oath is not sublime: we must consider the place, the manner, the circumstances, the motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oath should immortalize or suitably exalt its referents and be addressed to the appropriate object and moment (contrast Eupolis’s pointless oath with Demosthenes’ carefully designed oath). Tailor an oath to the feelings of the audience (e.g., defeated men) and avoid statements that invite obvious objections (Demosthenes avoids naming success to sidestep contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal the figure (hide artifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure is always most effective when it conceals the very fact of its being a figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brilliance and grandeur can obscure artifice so that devices are not recognized as devices. Use ornament and sublimity to throw rhetorical art into the shade so the effect strikes before the audience detects the device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obvious figures before authoritative audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures can suggest treachery, craft, or fallacy—especially when addressing judges, despots, or rulers—who resent being treated like children or outwitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use sophistic, conspicuous artifices with audiences likely to construe them as personal affronts; instead make the device appear natural or conceal it by grandeur to avoid provoking hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-and-answer to simulate spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The figures of question and answer brace language into greater vigour and rapidity and counterfeit spontaneous emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By asking and immediately answering questions (sometimes answering as if another had asked), a speaker makes premeditated arguments seem born in the moment, increasing force and apparent candour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asyndeton (omission) for agitation and rapidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases drop out unconnected in a sort of spate—almost too quick for the speaker—giving the idea of agitation which checks and hounds utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disconnected rapid phrases to convey excitement or haste (e.g., 'they pushed, fought, slew, fell'). Asyndeton speeds speech and suggests uncontrollable passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine figures for amplified effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of several figures (e.g., asyndeton, repetition, vivid presentation) often has a supremely moving effect, contributing force, conviction, and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave devices—repetition with asyndeta and vivid imagery—to sustain emotional momentum; their co-operation multiplies impact beyond isolated use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and continual variation to avoid monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotony expresses quiet, while emotion demands disorder; preserve essence of repetitions through continual variation so disorder implies order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat elements (manner, looks, voice) but vary them so the speech does not become a drone; variation sustains tension and prevents the effect from flattening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit connecting particles to preserve speed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rush and ruggedness of emotion is fined down and smoothed out by the use of connecting particles, it falls flat and loses its fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting conjunctions and smoothing devices when you want a bolt-from-the-catapult effect; connecting particles tie the motion and reduce immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (alter natural order) to imitate vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging words and thoughts out of the natural sequence bears the genuine stamp of vehement emotion and imitates how people speak when carried away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion to make speech seem wrung from the speaker (e.g., starting with fear then addressing audience). Long, risky inversions can compel audience excitement and simulate improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation, variation, climax (figures of many cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulation, variation, and climax are effective aids in giving ornament and every kind of sublime and emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting elements, raising intensity, and arranging variations in sequence can create a climactic impact; use changes in case/tense/person/number/gender for liveliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use number (plural vs singular) for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural sounds more full‑mouthed and suggests multitude; conversely contracting plurals to singular can give the sense of a single whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pluralization to magnify or magnify scale where heroics or exaggeration are invited; use singularization to compress separate individuals into a striking unity. Avoid routine overuse—reserve for appropriate emotional or rhetorical moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present past events as present for vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce events in past time as happening at the present moment to transform narrative into vivid actuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative becomes more immediate (e.g., 'Someone has fallen...') when past occurrence is rendered in present tense or as present action; commonly used by historians and poets to heighten drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of person/direct address to involve audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of person gives a vivid effect and often makes the audience feel themselves set in the thick of the danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressing the hearer as 'you' or appearing to speak to a single individual makes the audience more attentive and emotionally implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abrupt shift into a character's speech (change of speaker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden transition from narrator to a character's utterance is an outbreak of emotion; it anticipates a change of speaker and heightens immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tagging the speech with 'he said' when a crisis demands immediacy; let the narrative itself break into the character's voice for force (example: Hector’s abrupt cry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis (ornament) to enrich meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis contributes to the sublime; ornament enhances the beauty of the main theme and often chimes in with literal expression to give a richer note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circumlocution and ornamentation to complement meaning, but avoid bombast—ornament should sweeten and enrich, not overpower or make the passage pretentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary grammatical forms for liveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety and liveliness are lent to exposition by changes of case, tense, person, number, gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate shifts of grammatical forms (cases, tense shifts, person changes) can ornament text and convey nuance; use intentionally to animate prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint: avoid perpetual ornament (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamental devices should not be employed except where the subject invites heroics, redundance, exaggeration, or emotion; 'to jingle bells in every sentence would be unduly pretentious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint: do not parade stylistic devices mechanically or constantly, lest the effect become artificial and tedious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make devices appear natural (imitate nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is only perfect when it looks like nature; the best prose uses inversions and irregularities to imitate genuine human emotion and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for devices that mirror spontaneous utterance; the more your art conceals itself by resembling natural expression, the more persuasive and sublime it will seem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures to mask logical artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublimity and the effect on the emotions are a wonderfully helpful antidote against the suspicion that accompanies the use of figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a figure might be suspected of fallacy, surround it with grandeur and emotion so that its artfulness is less obvious; brilliance can neutralize suspicion of trickery.
